lab_title: Shapes of Molecules: Predicting Geometry with VSEPR Theory
top_level_objectives: Explain the central premise of VSEPR theory: that electron domains around a central atom orient to minimize mutual repulsion
Translate a Lewis structure into a count of bonding and lone-pair electron domains around a central atom
Identify the five fundamental electron-domain geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) and their idealized bond angles
Predict how lone pairs modify electron-domain geometry to yield molecular shapes such as bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, and square pyramidal
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing measurable deviations from idealized bond angles
Compare VSEPR predictions against the observed structures of real molecules (water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, XeF4)

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce VSEPR's central premise by letting students physically feel that electron domains push apart to minimize repulsion, setting up the entire lab.
key_visuals: A central atom rendered as a glowing sphere with a few attached electron-domain 'balloons' radiating outward
Repulsion force arrows or a color-coded strain meter that turns red when domains crowd and green when they spread out
A short animation of two, then three domains snapping into their lowest-energy angular arrangement
student_actions: Drag electron domains toward and away from one another and watch the repulsion/strain indicator respond in real time
Release the domains and observe them settle into a maximally separated arrangement
Read a brief caption summarizing the rule: electron domains arrange to be as far apart as possible

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Teach students to bridge a flat Lewis structure to a count of bonding and lone-pair domains around the central atom, the essential input for VSEPR.
key_visuals: A 2D Lewis structure of a simple molecule (e.g., water) floating beside its emerging 3D central atom
Highlighted bonding pairs and lone pairs, color-coded to distinguish them
A running tally showing 'bonding domains' and 'lone-pair domains' totaling the steric number
student_actions: Tap each bond and lone pair on the Lewis structure to classify it as a bonding or lone-pair domain
Confirm the total electron-domain count (steric number) for the central atom
Note that double and triple bonds count as a single domain

scenes.brief_purpose: Build a mental catalog of the five idealized geometries that arise from two through six electron domains, before lone pairs complicate them.
key_visuals: Five 3D models displayed in sequence: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral
Ideal bond-angle labels overlaid on each (180 degrees, 120 degrees, 109.5 degrees, 90/120 degrees, 90 degrees)
A rotating central atom that gains one domain at a time, morphing from one geometry to the next
student_actions: Step through the geometries by adding one electron domain at a time to the central atom
Rotate each 3D model to inspect its symmetry and measure the displayed bond angles
Match each domain count (2-6) to its correct geometry name in a quick check

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how replacing bonding domains with lone pairs transforms an electron-domain geometry into a distinct molecular shape.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral central atom whose bonding pairs are swapped one at a time for lone pairs, revealing trigonal pyramidal then bent shapes
Ghosted lone-pair domains shown as translucent lobes so the underlying electron geometry remains visible
Side-by-side labels distinguishing 'electron-domain geometry' from 'molecular geometry'
student_actions: Convert bonding domains into lone pairs and observe the molecular shape that the remaining atoms trace out
Toggle a view that hides the lone pairs to see only the atom positions
Identify the resulting molecular geometry name (e.g., bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal)

scenes.scene_name: Why Lone Pairs Bend the Angles
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain the subtle bond-angle deviations from ideal values by showing that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
key_visuals: A comparison of methane (109.5 degrees), ammonia (107 degrees), and water (104.5 degrees) with animated angle measurements
A fatter, closer translucent lobe representing the lone pair pressing bonding pairs together
A dynamic protractor showing the H-X-H angle shrinking as lone pairs are added
student_actions: Add lone pairs to a central atom and watch the measured bond angle compress below the idealized value
Compare the water, ammonia, and methane angles and rank them
Explain in a short prompt why the angle decreases as lone-pair count rises

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by applying the full VSEPR workflow to real molecules and confirming predictions against observed structures.
key_visuals: A gallery of real molecules to build: water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4
A prediction panel where the student's chosen geometry is checked against the accepted molecular shape
3D ball-and-stick models that assemble into their correct final geometries once predicted
student_actions: Select a molecule, count its electron domains, and predict its molecular geometry from memory
Watch the model assemble and compare the prediction to the observed structure
Complete a summary table matching each molecule to its electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and bond angle
